title: Feeling isn't consenting (IV.3)
hookLine: a thought you never invited shows up; a saint asks where Christ was during hers, and the answer is strange
tomorrow: after sin, what does Francis call the worst thing for a soul?

lines: WHAT KIND OF PERSON THINKS THAT?
WHERE WERE YOU? IN YOUR HEART.
cards: A thought shows up that nobody invited. A flash of wanting to trip the player who just beat you. A cruel line you'd never say out loud.
And then the second thought: what kind of person even thinks that? Francis de Sales answers with a strange story. Catherine of Siena, a saint, is flooded with ugly temptations she hates.
When they finally pass, she asks Christ where he was while her heart was full of darkness. His answer is the odd part. In your heart.

teach.b: How can Christ be in a heart full of thoughts like that? Francis solves it by slowing temptation down. First, something is suggested: the thought arrives.
Then a person may feel a pull, even a pleasure, in it. Then comes consent, or refusal.
Sin, in his account, lives at that last step, the yes. So a temptation can last a long time, he says, and do no harm, as long as it displeases us and we don't consent. That's the key to Catherine.
She hated those thoughts and kept saying no.
The fight itself showed her heart hadn't given way, and that, Christ tells her, is where he was: in the middle of the struggle, not outside it waiting.
The letter of James says something close: blessed is the one who endures temptation and comes through.
The temptation isn't the failure. Enduring it is part of the life. Here's a sentence a parent could say at dinner: having a mean thought is not the same as being mean.
None of this makes temptation small. It just moves the line to where Francis puts it, at the yes.

how: Catholic moral teaching distinguishes temptation from sin: a temptation that is resisted is not a sin to confess, and in the Lord's Prayer Catholics ask not to be led into temptation.

o: a temptation is fine if nobody sees it
you can't be blamed for anything you want
a pull felt but not chosen isn't a sin

games.q: feeling isn't consenting — tap the pairs.
p: where sin begins, in his account

s: feeling a temptation is already a sin
for Francis, sin begins at consent. a pull that displeases you and gets no yes does no harm.
a temptation can last a long time and still do no harm
as long as it displeases us and we don't consent, he says.
Christ tells Catherine he was absent during her dark thoughts
he says he was in her heart, in the middle of the struggle.

games.q: a friend who prays every day says if God were really with her, she wouldn't still be tempted. what does Catherine's story suggest?
o: the struggle itself can be where he is closest.
real holiness means the temptations stop for good.
the temptations mean God has stepped away for a while.
games.why: Catherine was tempted long and hard. Christ said he was in her heart the whole time; her hatred of the thoughts showed it.

practice: Close your eyes and let thoughts come and go. When one pulls at you, a craving, a grudge, a shortcut, name it plainly, a pull, and no yes, then come back to the breath without shame.

wordCard.voice: Feeling isn't consenting. A temptation felt is not a temptation chosen; for Francis, the line sits at the yes.

carryVoice: Your line: feeling isn't sin. The pull is real; the yes is yours to give or keep. Rest well tonight.
